Yes — Turso powers production applications today at multiple organizations, including Turso Cloud, the Kin AI assistant, and Spice.ai. Reliability is our top priority: Turso is extensively tested by a collection of tools including a native Deterministic Simulation Testing suite and Antithesis.

Turso is compatible with SQLite at the SQL dialect, file format, and C API levels, and existing SQLite database files work as-is. We are not at 100% yet, so some differences are still expected — COMPAT.md tracks the details — but the gap is closing quickly, and full compatibility is a requirement for 1.0.

Like SQLite, Turso compiles a query into bytecode for a virtual machine called the VDBE, and runs that bytecode. SQL is just one language that compiles to it. Our goal is to make that VM a general target, with one modern and rigorously tested core, and many database frontends compiled onto it: SQLite, Postgres, and others over time. LLVM did this for compilers, where a stable intermediate representation let many languages share one backend, and we think databases deserve the same. The bytecode is general enough to run Doom, if you want proof.

Rewriting SQLite in Rust started as an unassuming experiment, and due to its incredible success, replaces libSQL as our intended direction. Both run in production today: libSQL has been battle-tested for longer, while Turso Database is where our development effort is focused and is evolving rapidly. More details here.

Simkl uses explicit user/media-event checks, persisted activity cursors and baseline/delta observations, with durable watched writes confirmed by provider readback. Unsafe baseline observations stay available to explicit full-sync previews without filling Sync Attention; unsafe new deltas remain visible for review. Eligible concurrent writes share batches of up to 100 with a quota reserve; uncertain outcomes stay held without automatic resend. Ratings that could create watched/list state, unresolved anime/special identity, list-destructive unwatches, paid rewatches and automatic absence reconciliation remain blocked. Plekt retains its full local history independently of provider limits.

Bulk manual watched actions gather Simkl writes into chunks of up to 100, independently of LAN concurrency, and queued captured intents gather up to 100 per run with individual watch-row outcomes. Single watches remain immediate. Batch preflights respect the known quota reserve; failed or invalid preflights save a hold until quota reset, surviving restarts. Four requests apply per chunk; unrelated sequential watches can form separate chunks. Manual full sync requires a one-hour item preview with deselection, fresh-state rechecks and a verified backup. First-run selected history imports start on Continue without a separate preview approval, retaining the backup and freshness guards. Selected imports propagate to their listed media-server destinations; dates already on a destination are preserved. Simkl selected sends show request estimates and retain the quota reserve. Sends audited as missing from Simkl's current progress remain held for review and skipped by later previews. Incremental checks read a separate ratings delta only when rating activity changes, so rating-only edits and explicit clears are captured. After first-run imports finish, the add-only initial outward pass exposes per-destination progress and remaining or held items above Sync / Idle.

rekal is an MCP server that gives AI coding agents persistent memory across sessions. Memories are stored locally in SQLite and retrieved with hybrid search (BM25 keywords + vector semantics + recency decay). Nothing leaves your machine.
How it works · Quickstart · Install · Setup · Updating · Tools · Under the hood · Troubleshooting
Works with any MCP-capable agent: Claude Code, Codex CLI, OpenCode, Cursor CLI.
All state is a single file: `~/.rekal/memory.db`. For the scoring formula, schema, and embedding model, see Under the hood.
Requires Python 3.11+. On first run, rekal creates `~/.rekal/memory.db`. To upgrade an existing install later, see Updating.

`--scope user` registers rekal for all your projects. Without it, `claude mcp add` defaults to local scope and the server loads only in the project where you ran it (MCP scopes), and memory should follow you everywhere. The `--` separates Claude Code's own flags from the command that launches the server; stdio is the default transport.
Why disable built-in memory, and what if I forget?

**Why is this required?** Left enabled, Claude Code's built-in auto memory competes with rekal. It loads its own memory into the agent's context (context layout) and the agent favors it, writing everything to a flat file that cannot be searched, deduplicated, or ranked. Disabling it (`autoMemoryEnabled: false`, settings docs) removes the competitor. The plugin's hooks then re-assert rekal: SessionStart establishes that memory lives in rekal, and UserPromptSubmit injects prompt-matched memories on every turn.

**Can the plugin do this automatically?** No. Claude Code only lets a plugin's `settings.json` set the `agent` and `subagentStatusLine` keys (plugin settings); it cannot touch `autoMemoryEnabled`. This manual step is the only way.
What the plugin provides : hooks and skills

|session-start|`SessionStart`|`rekal hook session-start` injects a directive that memory lives only in rekal. It deliberately injects no memories: with no prompt yet there is nothing to match against, and recency-ordered recall was usually the wrong topic|

|user-prompt-submit|`UserPromptSubmit`|`rekal hook user-prompt-submit` recalls memories matching the submitted prompt (hybrid search, in-process) and injects the top matches under `## rekal memory`, so recall re-anchors to what you just asked on every turn|
|pre-compact|`PreCompact` (auto)|Runs a subagent that saves durable facts to rekal before context is compacted, so nothing is lost to summarization|

|session-end|`SessionEnd`|`rekal hook session-end` spawns a detached headless `claude -p` that saves durable facts to rekal when the session ends (agent hooks cannot run at SessionEnd — the REPL is already tearing down)|
|block-memory-writes|`PreToolUse` on Edit/Write|Denies writes to flat-file memory (MEMORY.md/.txt, memories.*) with a reason redirecting to rekal tools|
|redirect-memory-reads|`PreToolUse` on Read|Denies reads of flat-file memory and tells the agent to call `memory_build_context` instead, so a missing file no longer reads as "no memory exists"|
|`rekal-init`|`/rekal-init`|Scans codebase and bootstraps rekal with project knowledge|
|`rekal-save`|`/rekal-save` or auto on session end|Deduplicates and stores durable knowledge from the conversation|
|`rekal-usage`|`/rekal-usage`|Teaches agents how to use rekal effectively|
|`rekal-hygiene`|`/rekal-hygiene`|Finds conflicts, duplicates, and stale data, then proposes fixes|

The recall hooks run the released rekal from PyPI via `uvx --from rekal==<version> rekal hook <event>` (`uv` must be available; no separate `rekal` on the PATH needed). The pin matches the version this plugin commit was released as, so hooks and plugin stay in lockstep. uvx fetches the package once per version and caches the environment (tool environments are cached and reused across invocations), so nothing is built from the plugin copy, the warm path never resolves dependencies or touches the network, and the same command works on macOS, Linux, and Windows. Recall never blocks a session: a failed fetch (for example, offline first run) fails that hook non-blockingly and retries on the next one, and a missing DB, load error, or empty result degrades to injecting the directive alone.

Next, what happens inside one tool call, in How it works.

One tool call, step by step: the agent runs a tool, the PreToolUse hook denies a big Read and names the ctx_execute call, the MCP server runs it in the sandbox, SQLite FTS5 keeps the output, and after compaction a state block of at most 2,048 B comes back.

1. **Install.** Each agent's own install command adds the MCP server, the hooks and the skills `ctx-doctor`, `ctx-stats` and `ctx-upgrade` to that agent's config folder, for example `~/.codex/skills/<name>/SKILL.md`. `context-mode setup` writes or repairs any part the native command leaves out (ADR-0023).
2. **Session start.** The `SessionStart` hook opens the project database. When the session ran before, the agent gets one line that tells it to call `ctx_resume` (dispatch.ts).

3. **PreToolUse checks.** Before a tool runs, the `PreToolUse` hook checks the call in a fixed order: the user's deny list, WebFetch, curl and wget, inline HTTP and build commands, then a full-file Read over `OUTPUT_CAP` (16,384 B) and one-file shell dumps such as `cat` or `tail`. A Read with a line range runs as usual (decide.ts).

4. **The exact call.** When a check matches, the hook stops the call and its reply names the exact `ctx_*` call to use, for example `ctx_execute` with `{"language":"shell","code":"<the command>","intent":"<what you need>"}`. For WebFetch the reply names `ctx_index`, then `ctx_search` (read-deny.ts).

5. **The sandbox.** This is the Thinking in Code step: the agent's script runs here, and only what it prints comes back. `ctx_execute` writes the script to a temp folder and spawns the runtime from an argument list in the project folder. The timeout is `EXEC_TIMEOUT_MS` (600,000 ms, default and maximum); on timeout it stops the whole process group (`taskkill /F /T` on Windows). The child gets your environment minus preload variables such as `NODE_OPTIONS`, and the agent gets what the script prints, at most `OUTPUT_CAP` (execute.ts).

**Thinking in Code.** The agent sends a short script as a tool parameter, the script reads the data in the sandbox, and only what it prints goes into the context. Two real calls, in the form the Claude Code terminal shows them:
`ctx_execute` on 5,000 JSON records, from the Claude Code 2.1.312 stream of the Try-it run with Context Mode 2.0.0-next.26 (04-api-json.json). The data is 1,039,898 B; the agent gets 254 B.

`ctx_batch` on an install log and a long git log, one live MCP call to `release-out/server.mjs` of Context Mode 2.0.0-next.36 on 2026-11-03 (2026-11-03-ctx-batch.json). The commands print 228,881 B; the agent gets 8,667 B, the parts that match its two queries, and the full output stays in the index.

6. **Indexing.** The full output goes into the index in chunks of at most `MAX_CHUNK_BYTES` (4,096 B). A Markdown chunk stays inside one heading section, and a code block that fits stays whole. Each chunk goes into two SQLite FTS5 tables: a Porter-stemmed table for words and a trigram table for paths, names and parts of words (fts.ts).

`ctx_index` on a copy of this repo's `docs/how-it-works.md`, one live MCP call to `release-out/server.mjs` of Context Mode 2.0.0-next.36 on 2026-11-03 (calls.json). The file is 11,577 B; the agent gets 64 B.

7. **Search.** `ctx_search` ranks each table with BM25 and joins the two lists with Reciprocal Rank Fusion: a hit scores 1/(`RRF_K` + rank), with `RRF_K` = 60. Before it returns an empty list, it tries a spelling fix from the indexed words. Search covers this session, this worktree (the default) or the whole project, and each snippet is at most `SNIPPET_MAX_BYTES` (800 B) (search.ts).

`ctx_search` on that index, in the same run, in a project that also holds an `AGENTS.md`. One search reads the index and every agent's memory files. The agent gets 1,268 B: one content hit and one memory hit, each with its source and heading. For memory shared across machines, agents and sessions, see Context Mode Gateway Memory.

8. **Run, then replace.** On hosts that run the tool first, the `PostToolUse` hook checks the result. Output over `REPLACE_TRIGGER_BYTES` (4,096 B) goes into the index whole, and the agent gets the best-matching chunks and one `ctx_search` line for the rest (dispatch.ts).

9. **Journal and compaction.** The hooks log each prompt, edit, command, tool error and decision in a journal. After a compaction the agent gets a state block of at most `STATE_BUDGET` (2,048 B), and each long line becomes a `ctx_resume(seq)` pointer to the full row; one `ctx_resume` reply is at most `RESUME_CAP` (2,048 B). On the next prompt, a prompt-match block brings back the journal rows that match it by BM25 (ADR-0009).
`ctx_resume` with empty parameters returns the state block, in the same run: 209 B.

10. **The database.** Each project has one `context.db` under `~/.context-mode`, in Node's built-in `node:sqlite`. The database runs in WAL mode and runs a PASSIVE checkpoint on close. A new database gets built under a temp name and moves into place in one atomic step, and the busy timeout is `DB_TIMEOUT_MS` (5,000 ms) (db.ts).

11. **A hook error.** A hook always ends with exit 0. On any error it gives the host's allow reply and writes one log line to `~/.context-mode/hook-errors.log`, so your agent keeps working. A spawned hook has `HOOK_TIMEOUT_MS` (5,000 ms) (fallback.ts).
